_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
tosafot:a1.1: In brief: Teruma of the tithe too is taken by estimate and by thought. Question: the main source for “thought” is written about teruma of the tithe itself (“And your teruma shall be reckoned to you”, a verse addressed to the Levites), so why learn it from standard teruma? Answer: the verse says “as the grain of the threshing floor”, which is standard teruma, grain an Israelite separates from his threshing floor, so the matter is plainer there. Rashi in Gittin (31a) explained that teruma of the tithe learns only estimate from standard teruma, while thought is learned for both from “shall be reckoned”. It seems the Rabbis do not dispute Abba Elazar about thought, only about estimate. And if they do dispute, perhaps there is a reason not to apply the verse to teruma of the tithe even though it is written about it, as with taking from adjacent produce: the Yerushalmi (Terumot ch. 2) says teruma of the tithe teaches but does not learn, since “from it” is written about it yet is applied to standard teruma, and the Mishna (Bikkurim 2:5) teaches that teruma of the tithe, like first fruits, may be taken from pure for impure and not from adjacent produce. Gittin 30b (“were the ḥaverim suspected of taking teruma not from adjacent produce?”) Rabbeinu Tam explains as rabbinic, since by Torah law adjacency is not required. Still, it seems no one disputes thought, since Kiddushin 41b challenges the derivation of agency from teruma with “teruma is different, as it is taken by thought”, evidently according to everyone, and that is teruma of the tithe, where “you also” is written. But according to Rashi they do dispute thought, since our sugya sets Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda like Abba Elazar ben Gomel because of thought; that implies the Rabbis do not accept thought even for standard teruma, for otherwise even they could learn thought for tithe from the Merciful One calling it teruma. One can answer that the Merciful One called it teruma because of the teruma of the tithe within it. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a1.2: In brief: By thought: Rashi explained that he sets his eyes on this side [of the pile] as teruma and eats from that side, even though he did not separate. He seems to mean that because “shall be reckoned” is written, one may eat without separating, and may do so even in silence, setting his eyes on one side and eating from the other. Rashi gave another explanation: he thinks and says, “the two log that I will separate in the future”, though he now separates nothing; that is, speech is required, and permitting [eating] without separating is what is called “thought”; and we find speech called thought, as in Bava Metzia 44a on “for every matter of trespass”. It seems, though, that without speech too it is teruma, since the Mishna (Terumot 1:6) counts a mute among the five whose teruma is valid after the fact, and the Yerushalmi explains [the exclusion] as due to the blessing; and Shevuot 26b clearly implies it is valid when he resolved it in his heart, from “every generous heart”, saying that teruma and consecrated items are two verses that come as one, so oaths are not learned from them. Eating without separating poses no problem: everyone permits it, as in the case of one who buys wine from the Samaritans, which all permit but for the issue of retroactive clarification or the fear that the flask might burst; and in some places we permit second tithe “to its north”. Question: if teruma may be taken by setting the eyes on one side, why may one not separate terumot and tithes on a Festival? Shabbat 142a teaches that one may lift out [teruma from] a mixture of one in a hundred, and when it asks “but he is fixing it!” answers that this is Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon, who says one sets his eyes on one side and eats from the other, so it does not count as fixing. Answer: a mixture is different, as it was already fixed; the first fixing is not permitted on the grounds that it could be done by thought. Even demai may not be fixed on Shabbat (Shabbat 34a), though setting one’s eyes on one side and eating from the other is permitted for it, as shown in Ḥullin 6b about Rabbi Meir, who ate a vegetable leaf in Beit She’an. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:a1.1: Is juxtaposed: at the beginning of our chapter (above, 53a): “And your tithes”: the verse speaks of two tithes, one animal tithe and one grain tithe.
tosafot:a1.3: Animal tithe is juxtaposed to grain tithe: Rashi explained, from “You shall tithe a tithe”, as we say at the beginning of our chapter. One must say that [Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda] does not hold what [Rava] says: “I juxtaposed it for the year and not for anything else.” Further, at the beginning of our chapter we expound a different juxtaposition, “and there you shall bring … your tithes”, according to Rabbi Akiva, and perhaps it was juxtaposed only with regard to bringing. But according to Rava it is difficult: how does he explain the reason of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda? Likewise in Zevaḥim (45a) we expound that the consecrated animals of gentiles do not make a substitute, because substitution is juxtaposed to animal tithe and animal tithe to grain tithe, and with grain tithe “the children of Israel” is written, not gentiles. One can answer: [Rava] says “I juxtaposed it for the year and not for anything else” only with regard to tithing from one onto another, for example from one kind onto another that is not its kind, which is like new onto old.
gershom:a1.1: And animal tithe is juxtaposed to grain tithe: as it is written, “You shall tithe a tithe”: the verse speaks of two tithes, and so on. And in the Sifrei it is written: “And your teruma shall be reckoned to you” [“your teruma”, and not “the teruma”]: the verse speaks of two terumot, and so on. Just as standard teruma is taken by measure [our daf: by estimate] and by thought, so too teruma of the tithe.
rashi:a2.1: Sacred of its own accord: if he counted the ten [that is, counted toward the tenth] and the tenth was left in the pen, even though it did not come out and he did not count it, it is sacred of its own accord.
gershom:a2.1: It is sacred of its own accord: even if he did not call it “tenth” and did not call it “sacred”.
rashi:a3.1: But perhaps it is “tenth” that he did not call it: [a first explanation:] the Merciful One did not call it “tenth”, so as to give it the law of tithe, to be taken up to Jerusalem and sacrificed; the Merciful One called it merely “sacred”, meaning that sanctity takes effect on it and it is eaten only with its blemish. Another explanation: “but perhaps he did not call it tenth”: he did not give it the name “tenth”, but did call it “sacred”, and that is why it is tithe; but where he did not name it at all, it would not be sacred like other tithe. This [second explanation] is not from the mouth of my teacher.
rashi:a4.1: That the tenth was selected for him: since it came out at the end of nine, it is selected of itself as the tenth, so it is like other tithe even though he did not name it. Alternatively, the baraita deals with a case where he pointed at it: when it came out he pointed at it with his finger to make it tithe, only he did not speak with his mouth. But where it was left in the pen and he did not name it, we have not yet heard that it is sacred like other tithe.
gershom:a3.1: That the tenth was selected for him: it went outside, and he did not call it anything but was silent.
gershom:a4.1: Alternatively, that he pointed at it: he signaled with his hand [at it] that it is the tenth.
rashi:a5.1: The ninth is eaten with its blemish: since he called it “tenth”, for exchanging the name of tithe sanctifies [the animals] before it and after it, as below [60a]. But the others, at any rate, were not exempted then, since it is the ninth in the count of the animals.
rashi:a5.2: And all are exempt: the eight that had already come out.
rashi:a5.3: That the tenth became sacred: of its own accord, in the pen, even though it did not come out.
rashi:a6.1: Through a fit tally: when nine came out through the opening there was a count there fit to be tithed, for the tenth still existed and was fit to come out after them and exempt them; and since it was fit to come out, it is as though it had already come out and exempted the count. The reason is explained below [59b]. But the tenth itself, at any rate, was not sacred until it came out.
gershom:a5.1: But perhaps they were exempted through a fit tally: when these came out, the tenth in the pen was still alive and fit to complete their count. That is why they are exempt, and not because they are definitely tithed.
rashi:a7.1: And the tenth is tithe: evidently, even though it did not come out, it is sacred of its own accord in the pen. Now [the Gemara] challenges this baraita, which teaches that the ninth is eaten with its blemish: “But isn’t it taught…”
gershom:a6.1: Whose is this? [The baraita that disagrees] that the ninth is eaten with its blemish is Rabbi Shimon’s, [in a case] where the name of “tenth” was not removed from the tenth.
rashi:b1.1: Even the ninth: just as, if he called the eleventh “tenth”, it is not sacred unless the name of tithe was removed from the tenth, that is, he did not call the tenth “tenth” but “ninth”, as we say below in the mishna (60a), “This is the principle: wherever the name of tenth was not removed…”, and the latter part of this baraita explains the reason, because the eleventh produces sanctity to be sacrificed, or alternatively because with the eleventh [the tenth] was already selected: so too the ninth, if he called it “tenth”, will not be eaten only with its blemish unless the name of the tenth was removed from the tenth, for example he called it “ninth”. Therefore here, where it was not removed, we say the ninth is non-sacred. “And logic dictates”: with the ninth too we require that the name of tenth be removed “from it”, that is, from the tenth itself.
gershom:b1.1: Even the ninth is not sacred: [not sacred] to be eaten only with its blemish. [Rabbi Shimon] speaks of the latter clause of the mishna.
gershom:b2.1: Unless the name of the tenth was removed from it: from the tenth, that is, he did not call the tenth “tenth”. But if he called the definite tenth “tenth”, the ninth is non-sacred.
rashi:b2.1: To be sacrificed: as we say below (60a), that if he called the eleventh “tenth” it is sacrificed as a peace offering, and we derive it from a verse. And even though it is so stringent, it is sacred only if the name of tenth was removed from the tenth, for example he called the tenth “ninth”, as we say below: “This is the principle…”
rashi:b2.2: The ninth: which is so lenient.
rashi:b2.3: Which does not produce sanctity to be sacrificed: even though he called it “tenth”, it is not sacrificed; it is sacred only for this alone, that it is eaten only with its blemish, as below. Is it not logical, and so on.
rashi:b2.4: If not, not: it would not be sacred at all.
gershom:b3.1: And logic dictates: if the eleventh, which produces sanctity to be sacrificed, as we say in the mishna, “and the eleventh is sacrificed as a peace offering”, is not sacred unless the name of the tenth was removed from the tenth, as we learned: he called the ninth “tenth” and the tenth “tenth” [and the eleventh “tenth”, the eleventh is not sanctified]…
rashi:b3.1: That itself provides: the Gemara replies that with the ninth it is certainly logical that its sanctity takes effect on it even though the name of tenth was not removed from [the tenth]. For with the eleventh it is logical that if [the name] was removed, yes, and if not, not, because its sanctity is stringent, as it is sacrificed, as below; so it is logical to require removal before that stringent sanctity takes effect.
rashi:b3.2: But the ninth: whose sanctity is light, as it is not sacred to be sacrificed but only so that it is eaten only with its blemish: it is logical that this light sanctity takes effect through a light thing, such as his calling it “tenth”, even though the name of tithe was not removed from the tenth itself.
gershom:b4.1: That itself provides: that is, from that very argument you bring, we learn that the ninth is sacred even though the name of tenth was not removed from the tenth.
rashi:b4.1: Alternatively: one can give another reason.
rashi:b5.1: The eleventh, for which the tenth was selected: the tenth had already come out before the eleventh came out, and was selected of itself as tithe. So it is logical that the eleventh not be sacred even though he called it “tenth”, unless the name of tithe was removed from the tenth: after a complete tenth, how could there be another tenth right next to it?
rashi:b5.2: Even though he did not remove it: and he went and called this one “tenth”.
rashi:b5.3: There is nothing more: nothing can be said against this argument he made, “that itself provides”, for it is certainly logical that [the ninth] be sacred even though [the name] was not removed.
gershom:b5.1: For which the tenth was selected, as it had already come out. [But the ninth,] for which the tenth was not yet selected, as it had not yet come out, is sacred even though the name of tenth was not removed from it, since he did not name the one left in the pen.
rashi:b6.1: A fit tally exempts: if he had ten lambs, brought them into the pen and counted nine or eight, and one of those remaining in the pen died, or went out through another opening so that the tenth was not sanctified, those he already counted are exempt because they are a fit tally: when he counted them, those in the pen were fit to come out and the tenth be tithed together with these for the count. Here it implies to us that [the exemption] is from that same count, which he has not yet completed, having counted only nine or eight, as I explained above.
rashi:b6.2: Among them: into the pen. All are exempt because they became mixed, for those already counted are exempt even though he has not yet tithed for them.
gershom:b6.1: Is it not that they were exempted through a fit tally: when they came out of the pen, there was still [an animal] left in the pen that could complete their count.
rashi:b7.1: But perhaps he tithed for them: and that is what “from the counted” means, that is, from those he counted and tithed for.
gershom:b7.1: But perhaps: you cannot [prove it] from here, for perhaps it speaks of counted animals for which he had already tithed, which jumped in.
gershom:b8.1: You cannot say that: for it goes on to teach “from the tithed”; evidently the “counted” it speaks of are not tithed.
rashi:b9.1: Tithed: that is, from the tithes themselves.
rashi:b9.2: Must graze: because about each and every one there is a doubt that it is the tithe.
gershom:b9.1: But perhaps, what does “from the tithed” mean? That the tithe itself jumped in.
gershom:b10.1: It is also precise, since it teaches “must graze”: for all of them are possibly tithe. And “from the counted” refers to those for which he had already tithed. So we still cannot derive from here that a fit tally exempts.
rashi:b10.1: Rather, is it not that they were exempted, and so on: for this is what it implies: “and not that which already passed” through a fit [tally], that at the time it passed it was fit to be tithed together with those in the pen; that one is certainly [exempt], because it was exempted through a fit tally.
gershom:b11.1: Rather, Rava said: he derives it from a verse, as it is written “passes”, and not what has already passed.
rashi:b11.1: And he counted five: “five” is not meant precisely.
rashi:b11.2: The counted are exempt: because they were a fit tally.
gershom:b12.1: If one of the counted died: of those that came out of the pen, what of it? He counts and completes over them and over the one that died until there are ten, and separates one.
gershom:b13.1: And if one of those not counted died: of those in the pen.
gershom:b14.1: The counted that went outside are exempt: the fit tally exempted them, for when they came out [the one] had not yet died and was fit to complete their count to ten. And those not counted, the four left in the pen, are not exempted but combine for another gathering, to be tithed with other animals.
rashi:b12.1: Through this opening: for the pen had two openings.
rashi:b12.2: He takes one of them: since ten came out through that opening.
rashi:b12.3: And the remainder: the four that came out through the other opening combine for another gathering. They cannot be exempted through a fit tally, for when they came out through their opening there was no fit tally: only four were left in the pen, and four with four cannot combine to be subject to tithe.
rashi:b13.1: But if not: the four did not come out through the opening of the six, but either remained in the pen or came out through the opening of the other four.
rashi:b13.2: The first four and the six are exempt: because when the four came out first they were a fit tally, for ten still remained in the pen, fit to combine with them and be tithed for them. And the last four, which remained or came out through a third opening, combine for another gathering. [This note explains the second case, Rava’s “but if not” in 59b14.]
gershom:b15.1: But if not: they did not come out through the opening where the six came out but through the opening of the four, so that now there are eight [there], not fit for tithe.
gershom:b16.1: The six that came out first are exempt: because when they came out of the pen, there remained in the pen a count fit to complete them to ten. And these four and those four combine for another gathering.
gershom:b17.1: Four came out: first, through this opening, and so on.
gershom:b18.1: He takes one as tithe and the rest are exempt: even the four that came out first, because they were exempted through a fit tally.
gershom:b19.1: But if not: [the last four] came out only through the opening of the four. The first four and the second six are exempt, because there remained in the pen [enough] fit to complete them.
gershom:b20.1: And these last four combine for another gathering.
rashi:b15.1: If those six that remained came out through one of their openings: that is, through the opening of the first four or through the opening of the last four.
rashi:b15.2: He takes one of them: because there are ten at one opening.
rashi:b15.3: But if not: they came out neither through the opening of these four nor through the opening of those four, but by themselves, or they remained in the pen.
rashi:b15.4: The first four and the last four are exempt: for each group of four that came out left others behind enough to combine with them and be tithed for them, since the six that remained can be assigned both here and there.
gershom:b21.1: If those six all came out through one opening, either the opening of the first four or that of the second four, there are ten and he takes one of them, and all the rest are exempt, even the four through whose opening the six did not come out, because those [second four too], when they came out, were a fit tally. But if not, three of them came out through this opening and three through that one: each four is exempt, because they came out in a fit tally, and the six combine for another gathering.
rashi:b16.1: A definitely fit tally: for example, he counted five or six and enough remained in the pen to combine with them, and the pen has only that opening, so it is certain that those remaining are fit to come out through that same opening and be tithed together with those he already counted.
rashi:b16.2: But an uncertainly fit tally: for example, they came out through two openings, four through this opening and four through that one; with the six that remained, one cannot determine whether they will come out through this opening or that. Since it is uncertain, one might say we do not apply “fit tally” and assign them both here and there to exempt them all. [Rava] teaches us [that we do]. Another explanation: the very fact that they are fit for here and for there, so that we assign them both to these four and to those four, is what counts as “uncertain”. This is from the mouth of my teacher.
gershom:b22.1: Lest you say we apply only a definitely fit tally: for example, where six came out through this opening and four through that one, and four remained, it is certain that the four that remained are fit to combine only [with] the six. But an uncertainly fit tally, as when six remained in the pen, fit to combine either with these four or with those four, and we do not know with which: say we do not. [Rava] teaches us [that we do].
rashi:b17.1: Fifteen lambs: not meant precisely; it is just the usual way of putting it, combining five with five.
gershom:b23.1: And the rest are exempt: [he would claim] the five he did not bring in are exempt too, since they lack the minimum for tithe. Rather, let him act so that they all become obligated in tithe: bring them all into the pen, take out ten and take one of them; and the remaining five, since they entered the pen while lacking the minimum for tithe, the pen fixes them [as obligated], and they combine for another gathering.
